rv.q: Ali Bianchi’s movement – with Greenwood bouncing about the set, powered by passion, ambition and later anxiety, distress and fear – keeps the action kinetically vital.
This is a fantastic play about the complexities of life, reminding us that human beings are not and never will be linear.
A thoroughly enjoyable and refreshingly different theatrical experience.
Greenwood's well-written, entertaining and frequently gripping play exploring the blindness of love is cleverer than that, offering parallels not certainties.
Relative Motion may not be the most original play about an abusive partner, but it does what it does well.
While the writing remains fairly unremarkable throughout, the dynamics in Greenwood’s story make it more interesting as they develop.
This is an accomplished play that raises questions while presenting an assured script and characters.

There’s a really interesting tale of how a relationship turns toxic here, and the central actors are deeply compelling, but the high-concept nature of the structure works against itself, rather than with it.
There is clear potential in the idea, with some powerful and unsettling moments, but at this point the production does not quite sustain the momentum needed to bring all the elements together.
Here, Paul isn't manipulating Sam. Greenwood is manipulating Paul. The workings show.
Relative Motion is an enjoyable, well-performed exploration of the human mating ritual, with flashes of excellent comedy, a darker underlying message and an intriguing scientific premise.

cn.t: Critics give *Relative Motion* a mixed-to-warm reception, praising Greenwood's clever use of Newtonian physics to frame a coercive relationship, though some find it derivative. Strong performances elevate an uneven but often compelling debut.
